level1.text: The diameter of a red blood cell is $7.5\cdot10^{-6}\,\text{m}$. How many micrometres is that? One micrometre is $1\,\mu\text{m} = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}$.
The figure shows an axis of powers of ten for the size $d$, with a hydrogen atom and an ant marked on it. How many orders of magnitude are there between their sizes?
The diameter of Earth is $1.27\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m}$. Give it in kilometres.
The diameter of a lead atom is about $3.5\cdot10^{-10}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of its nucleus about $1.4\cdot10^{-14}\,\text{m}$. How many times larger is the atom than its nucleus?
The thickness of a hair is $7.0\cdot10^{-5}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of a red blood cell $7.5\cdot10^{-6}\,\text{m}$. How many times thicker is the hair than the red blood cell?

In physics, observations and models are different things. For example, an observation is that in air, a stone dropped from the same height at the same time as a feather hits the ground before the feather. Which of the following separates a physical model from a mere observation?
level1.answer: A prediction for a new situation can be deduced from a model, and the prediction can be tested by a measurement.

choices.text: A prediction for a new situation can be deduced from a model, and the prediction can be tested by a measurement.
choices.feedback: Correct: an observation tells what happened, whereas a model is a simplified description from which you can deduce what would happen in a new situation. A model is tested with experiments and measurements, and it holds only in certain conditions.

choices.text: A model is an observation that has been repeated so many times that it certainly holds in all conditions.
choices.feedback: A repeated observation is still an observation. A model describes a phenomenon and produces predictions, and its validity is limited to certain conditions: for example, a free-fall model that ignores air resistance does not describe the fall of a feather.

choices.text: A model is a theory that cannot be changed any more once it has been found to work.
choices.feedback: A model is not unchangeable: its range of validity is determined by experiments and measurements. When a new measurement differs from the prediction, the model is corrected or its range of validity is limited. For example, a free-fall model without air resistance describes a stone but not a feather.

choices.text: A model is a perfect description of a phenomenon, and if a measurement differs from it, the measurement is always wrong.
choices.feedback: A model is a simplification, not the whole truth. When a careful measurement differs from the model's prediction, the experiment decides: the model is corrected or its range of validity is limited, and the measurement is not rejected merely because it does not fit the model.

level1.text: The distance from the Earth to the Moon is on average $3.84\cdot10^{8}\,\text{m}$. The travel time of light is the distance divided by the speed, $t = s/c$. How long does light take to travel from the Earth to the Moon when the speed of light is $c = 2.998\cdot10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$?

The order of magnitude of the diameter of a grain of sand is $10^{-3}\,\text{m}$ and that of a virus $10^{-7}\,\text{m}$. Based on the orders of magnitude, how many times larger is a grain of sand than a virus?

Assume an eclipse in which the Moon just barely covers the Sun completely. The Sun and the Moon then look approximately equally large in the sky. The distance of the Moon from the Earth is $3.84\cdot10^{8}\,\text{m}$, the diameter of the Moon is $3.47\cdot10^{6}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of the Sun is $1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m}$.

An object looks equally large when its distance is as many times the distance of the Moon as its diameter is times the diameter of the Moon. Which value is a reasonable estimate for the distance of the Earth from the Sun?

choices.feedback: Correct: the diameter of the Sun is $1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m} : 3.47\cdot10^{6}\,\text{m}\approx400$ times the diameter of the Moon, so the Sun is about $400$ times farther away than the Moon: $3.84\cdot10^{8}\,\text{m}\cdot400\approx1.5\cdot10^{11}\,\text{m}$.

This is only about $4$ times the distance of the Moon, although the Sun is about $400$ times larger than the Moon. That close, the Sun would look about a hundred times larger than the Moon, and the Moon would not cover it in an eclipse.

This is less than half the distance of the Moon, so the Sun would be closer than the Moon and would look a thousand times larger than the Moon. If you remember the number $150$ million, it is the distance in kilometres; in metres it is $1.5\cdot10^{11}$.

This is about $39\,000$ times the distance of the Moon, although the diameter of the Sun is only about $400$ times the diameter of the Moon. That far away, the apparent diameter of the Sun would be about a hundredth of the apparent diameter of the Moon. The Moon would then easily cover the Sun completely, so the assumption of approximately equal apparent diameters would not hold.

level2.text: The diameter of the Milky Way is about $1.0\cdot10^{5}$ light-years, and one light-year is $9.46\cdot10^{15}\,\text{m}$. The diameter of the observable universe is about $8.8\cdot10^{26}\,\text{m}$. How many Milky Way diameters would fit in a row across the diameter of the observable universe? Give the answer in thousands.

Proxima Centauri is $4.0\cdot10^{16}\,\text{m}$ away. How many years does light take to travel the distance, when the speed of light is $2.998\cdot10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$ and one year is $3.156\cdot10^{7}\,\text{s}$?
The circumference of Earth is $4.0\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m}$. How many people $1.7\,\text{m}$ tall would have to be placed end to end for the line to reach around Earth? Give the answer in millions.

The diameter of the Sun is $1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of Earth $1.27\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m}$. The volume of a sphere is directly proportional to the third power of the diameter. How many times larger is the volume of the Sun than the volume of Earth? Give the answer in millions.

The table shows the mean distance $r$ of the planets from the Sun in astronomical units; one astronomical unit is $1\,\text{AU}$. It corresponds approximately to the mean distance of the Earth from the Sun.

A scale model of the solar system is drawn in a corridor so that Neptune is $2.0\,\text{m}$ from the Sun and all distances are reduced by the same factor.

How far from the Sun is Jupiter in the model? Give the answer in centimetres. Which planet is closest in the model to the point of the corridor that is $1.0\,\text{m}$ from the Sun?

data.caption: Distances of the planets from the Sun

level2.text: The table gives the size $d = a\cdot10^{n}\,\text{m}$ of four objects in powers-of-ten form. Determine the order of magnitude of each object and calculate how many orders of magnitude there are between a human and the Milky Way. Justify why the order of magnitude of the Milky Way is not $10^{20}$ although its exponent is $20$.

A single sheet of paper is much thinner than the scale division $1\,\text{mm}$ of a ruler, so its thickness cannot be measured directly.

A student stacked sheets of the same copy paper, pressed the stack lightly together and measured its height $h$ with a ruler, reading the result to half a millimetre. A stack of $N$ sheets has the height $h = dN$, where $d$ is the thickness of one sheet, so the points lie on a line that passes through the origin and whose slope is $d$.

Draw a graph of the points and fit a line to them. Read the height of the stack at $N = 300$ from the line and calculate the thickness $d$ of one sheet in millimetres by dividing the height by the number of sheets. Explain why measuring a stack gives a more accurate result than measuring a single sheet.

data.caption: Height of a paper stack as a function of the number of sheets

level3.text: We make a scale model in which Earth is a sphere with a diameter of $1.0\,\text{cm}$, and all other distances are drawn on the same scale. The distance of Earth from the Sun is $1.50\cdot10^{11}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of Earth $1.27\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m}$. How far from the sphere would the Sun be in the scale model?

The Planck length is $1.6\cdot10^{-35}\,\text{m}$, the size of a proton $1.7\cdot10^{-15}\,\text{m}$ and the height of a person $1.7\,\text{m}$. Which difference of orders of magnitude is larger: between the Planck length and the proton, or between the proton and a person? Give the larger difference as a number of powers of ten.

In a picture taken with an electron microscope, a virus with a diameter of $1.0\cdot10^{-7}\,\text{m}$ appears $5.0\,\text{cm}$ wide. The picture is not altered in any way. How wide would a red blood cell with a diameter of $7.5\cdot10^{-6}\,\text{m}$ appear in the same picture? Give the answer in centimetres.

Estimate how many raindrops fall on a football pitch during one rain shower.

Assumptions: the shower increases the thickness of the water layer on the pitch at the rate $5.0\,\text{mm/h}$ and lasts $10\,\text{min}$, the area of the pitch is $6.0\cdot10^{3}\,\text{m}^2$ and every drop is a sphere with a diameter of $2.0\,\text{mm}$. The volume of a sphere is $V = 4\pi r^{3}/3$.

How many drops fall on the pitch, in billions? Which of the assumptions affects the result most if its value is $20\,\%$ too large, and why? Justify by calculation.

Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause on 5 November 2018 at a distance $d_0 = 119.7\,\text{AU}$ from the Sun, and its speed relative to the Sun is $v = 15.341\,\text{km/s}$. The model of uniform motion is $d = d_0 + vt$.

A student calculated the model's prediction for February 2026, when $t = 7.25\,\text{a}$ has passed since the heliopause crossing. The student's solution: “The distance travelled is $s = vt = 15.341\,\text{km/s}\cdot7.25 = 111.2\,\text{km}$. The distance is $d = 119.7\,\text{AU} + 111.2\,\text{km} \approx 119.7\,\text{AU}$. So Voyager would be almost in the same place as in 2018, which means the model is wrong.”

Use the values $1\,\text{AU} = 1.496\cdot10^{8}\,\text{km}$ and $1\,\text{a} = 3.156\cdot10^{7}\,\text{s}$. A measurement in February 2026 gave $143.05\,\text{AU}$.

Find the student's error and calculate the correct prediction of the model for the distance $d$ in astronomical units. Explain why the measurement supports the model but does not prove that Voyager always moves at the same speed.
